resource.title: Kinwise visit brief: Margaret Rivera, Sep 12 through Oct 11

text.div: • Alex (daughter) wrote on Oct 4: "Mom seems foggier in the mornings since urgent care started the new sleeping pill. She almost fell in the bathroom on Wednesday."

• Dizziness was recorded on 9 of 14 answered days from Sep 25, when Lorazepam (Ativan) was started, through Oct 11, compared with 2 of 19 answered days in the 21 days before.
  • Daytime drowsiness was recorded on 8 of 14 answered days from Sep 25, when Lorazepam (Ativan) was started, through Oct 11, compared with 2 of 20 answered days in the 21 days before.
  • Confusion or memory fog was recorded on 4 of 14 answered days from Sep 25, when Lorazepam (Ativan) was started, through Oct 11, compared with 0 of 20 answered days in the 21 days before.
  • Around the start of Lorazepam (Ativan) on Sep 25, check-ins were recorded on 20 of 21 days before (Sep 4 through Sep 24) and on 14 of 17 days after (Sep 25 through Oct 11).
  • From Sep 25, when Lorazepam (Ativan) was started, through Oct 11: 1 fall (Oct 6) and 2 near-falls (Sep 27, Sep 30) were recorded on 14 answered days, compared with 1 near-fall (Sep 11) on 20 answered days in the 21 days before.

These are home records. They show what was recorded, not why.

• Lorazepam (Ativan): benzodiazepine. AGS Beers 2023 lists Lorazepam (Ativan) as a medicine older adults should generally avoid. (AGS Beers Criteria® 2023)
  • Tylenol PM (OTC): sedating (first-generation) antihistamine. AGS Beers 2023 lists the diphenhydramine in Tylenol PM (OTC) as a medicine older adults should generally avoid. (AGS Beers Criteria® 2023)
  • Anticholinergic burden score (ACB): 7. Margaret's medicines add up to 7 on the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale, a published list of medicines with anticholinergic effects: the diphenhydramine in Tylenol PM (OTC) 3, Oxybutynin 3 and Furosemide (Lasix) 1. (ACB scale, 2012 update)
  • Medicines linked to falls, with falls or dizziness recorded (5). 5 of Margaret's medicines are on published lists of medicines linked to falls in older adults (CDC STEADI-Rx and STOPPFall 2021): Lorazepam (Ativan), Furosemide (Lasix), Amlodipine, Tylenol PM (OTC) and Oxybutynin. (CDC STEADI-Rx; STOPPFall 2021)
  • Possible prescribing cascade: Amlodipine → ankle swelling → Furosemide (Lasix). Furosemide (Lasix) was started on Jul 8, 45 days after Amlodipine, for “ankle swelling”. (Savage 2020)

11 screening prompts are included as DetectedIssue resources. They are questions to ask, not instructions.

1. Could Lorazepam (Ativan) be contributing to the dizziness, daytime drowsiness, confusion or memory fog, falls and near-falls recorded in the diary since Sep 25?
  2. Is Lorazepam (Ativan) still the best option for sleep or anxiety, and are there alternatives with less effect on balance and memory?
  3. Could Tylenol PM (OTC) be contributing to the dizziness, daytime drowsiness, confusion or memory fog, falls and near-falls recorded in the diary in the last 30 days?
  4. Margaret's anticholinergic burden score (ACB) adds up to 7. Could any of these medicines be reduced or replaced with one that has less anticholinergic effect?
  5. Could any of the medicines linked to falls be contributing to the falls, near-falls and dizziness recorded from Sep 12 through Oct 11, and could Margaret's list be reviewed for fall risk?

  • This review checks published criteria (AGS Beers 2023, ACB scale, fall-risk medicines, known prescribing cascades). It does not check doses, kidney function unless provided, allergies, or every interaction. No flag is not an all-clear for any medicine.

Lorazepam (Ativan): benzodiazepine.

AGS Beers 2023 lists Lorazepam (Ativan) as a medicine older adults should generally avoid. Older adults are more sensitive to benzodiazepines, which are linked to memory problems, confusion, falls, broken bones and car crashes; after regular use they should be reduced gradually with the prescriber rather than stopped suddenly. For the clinician: Older adults have increased sensitivity and slower metabolism of long-acting agents; any benzodiazepine raises the risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures and motor vehicle crashes, plus abuse, misuse and dependence. Combined with opioids: profound sedation and respiratory depression. Evidence: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023 · strong recommendation · moderate-quality evidence. Source: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023. Question for the visit: Could Lorazepam (Ativan) be contributing to the dizziness, daytime drowsiness, confusion or memory fog, falls and near-falls recorded in the diary since Sep 25? Is Lorazepam (Ativan) still the best option for sleep or anxiety, and are there alternatives with less effect on balance and memory? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

text.div:
Tylenol PM (OTC): sedating (first-generation) antihistamine.

AGS Beers 2023 lists the diphenhydramine in Tylenol PM (OTC) as a medicine older adults should generally avoid. This older antihistamine, the sleep ingredient in many “PM” and night-time products, can lead to next-day drowsiness, confusion, constipation and trouble passing urine, and its sleep effect fades with regular use. For the clinician: Highly anticholinergic; clearance falls with age and tolerance develops to the hypnotic effect. Cumulative anticholinergic exposure is associated with falls, delirium and dementia (acute use for a severe allergic reaction may be appropriate). Evidence: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023 · strong recommendation · moderate-quality evidence. Source: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023. Question for the visit: Could Tylenol PM (OTC) be contributing to the dizziness, daytime drowsiness, confusion or memory fog, falls and near-falls recorded in the diary in the last 30 days? Is the sedating antihistamine in Tylenol PM (OTC) still needed, or is there a gentler option for sleep or allergies? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

text.div:
Furosemide (Lasix): check sodium levels.

AGS Beers 2023 lists Furosemide (Lasix) as a medicine to use with caution in older adults. This medicine can lower the sodium level in the blood, which can lead to confusion, unsteadiness and falls, especially when it is started or the dose changes. For the clinician: Use with caution: may exacerbate or contribute to SIADH or hyponatremia; monitor sodium closely when starting or changing dosages. Evidence: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023 · strong recommendation · moderate-quality evidence. Source: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023. Question for the visit: Could Furosemide (Lasix) be contributing to the dizziness, falls and near-falls recorded in the diary in the last 30 days? Has Margaret's sodium level been checked since Furosemide (Lasix) was started or the dose last changed? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

text.div:
2 medicines with strong anticholinergic effects together.

AGS Beers 2023 lists taking 2 or more medicines with strong anticholinergic effects together as a combination older adults should generally avoid; Margaret takes 2: the diphenhydramine in Tylenol PM (OTC) and Oxybutynin. For the clinician: Avoid; minimize the number of anticholinergic drugs: increased risk of cognitive decline, delirium, falls and fractures. Evidence: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023 · strong recommendation · moderate-quality evidence. Source: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023. Question for the visit: Are all of these medicines with anticholinergic effects still needed together, and could any be replaced with one that has less anticholinergic effect? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

Anticholinergic burden score (ACB): 7.

Margaret's medicines add up to 7 on the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale, a published list of medicines with anticholinergic effects: the diphenhydramine in Tylenol PM (OTC) 3, Oxybutynin 3 and Furosemide (Lasix) 1. The scale's authors treat a total of 3 or more as worth reviewing, because these effects (such as dry mouth, constipation, drowsiness and confusion) add up across medicines. For the clinician: ACB total 7 (high; diphenhydramine 3, oxybutynin 3, furosemide 1). In observational studies, ACB totals of 3 or more were associated with cognitive impairment and higher mortality; the scale is not a prediction for an individual. Source: ACB scale, 2012 update. Question for the visit: Margaret's anticholinergic burden score (ACB) adds up to 7. Could any of these medicines be reduced or replaced with one that has less anticholinergic effect? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

text.div:
Possible prescribing cascade: Amlodipine → ankle swelling → Furosemide (Lasix).

Furosemide (Lasix) was started on Jul 8, 45 days after Amlodipine, for “ankle swelling”. Ankle swelling (peripheral edema) is a known possible effect of amlodipine-type medicines; a new medicine started for an effect like this is called a prescribing cascade. For the clinician: Amlodipine started May 24; Furosemide (Lasix) started Jul 8 (+45 days) for “ankle swelling”. Dihydropyridine CCB edema is driven by arteriolar vasodilation and responds poorly to diuretics; new loop diuretic dispensing after CCB initiation is a documented cascade (Savage 2020). Source: Savage 2020. Question for the visit: Could the ankle swelling be linked to Amlodipine, and is Furosemide (Lasix) still the best way to manage it? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

Dihydropyridine CCB edema is driven by arteriolar vasodilation and responds poorly to diuretics; new loop diuretic dispensing after CCB initiation is a documented cascade (Savage 2020). Source: Savage 2020. Question for the visit: Could the ankle swelling be linked to Amlodipine, and is Furosemide (Lasix) still the best way to manage it? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.

Omeprazole: acid reducer (PPI) for more than 8 weeks.

AGS Beers 2023 lists Omeprazole as a medicine older adults should generally avoid when taken daily for more than 8 weeks. Taking an acid reducer like this every day for more than 8 weeks is linked to a serious gut infection (Clostridioides difficile), pneumonia, bone loss and fractures. For the clinician: Avoid scheduled use for more than 8 weeks unless high risk (oral corticosteroids, chronic NSAID use), erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, a pathologic hypersecretory condition, or demonstrated need for maintenance. Risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, pneumonia, GI malignancy, bone loss and fractures. Evidence: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023 · strong recommendation · high-quality evidence. Source: AGS Beers Criteria® 2023. Question for the visit: Does Margaret still need Omeprazole every day, and could the plan for it be reviewed? A screening prompt from published criteria, not a clinical judgment.
